prize_parts.citation: For introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting and foreign investment in trade theory, thereby identifying reallocation across firms as a channel for the gains from trade and opening a firm-level empirical agenda.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B001 alone, credited to Helpman and Melitz. The case is the content of the discovery. Melitz (2003) and Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) moved trade analysis from sectors and representative firms to firms that differ in productivity and sort into exporting, foreign investment or neither. This gives a tractable account of reallocation as a channel for the gains from trade, with predictions that more than twenty years of firm-level data from many countries have tested and refined. From my own field I see this as more than a trade result. Selection and reallocation across heterogeneous firms are now routine in macro, growth and productivity work, including the misallocation and creative-destruction literatures I follow. This is a judgment about conceptual reach, not about how many colleagues ranked the entry first, and the chair is right that our agreement is not independent evidence, since the eleven files share a model and reasoning habits. The round-1 exchange did not change my view of the science. It changed how I would word the citation, and it changed my alternatives. I would limit the citation to selection into exporting and investment and to reallocation across firms. It should claim neither a settled size of the welfare gains nor the whole firm-level and quantitative trade literature. A single part is also the right structure. B001 uses two of the three laureate slots, and a second part would need a distinct achievement with at most one person. No shortlisted candidate offers that without fragmenting its credit, for example Pakes alone in B006.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still attribution, and I now weigh it more heavily than in round 1. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are outside the credited names, and Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum (2003) is a contemporaneous heterogeneous-producer model that is not merely the Eaton-Kortum Ricardian framework. Bernard and Jensen's exporter-premia facts also helped create the empirical question. If the Committee defines the discovery as the combination of those facts, the theory and the quantification, this entry is too narrow and a two-name award would be hard to defend. Redding's quantitative and spatial work is also excluded. The baseline model's sharper predictions are rejected in detail, and its welfare implications depend on distributional and functional-form assumptions. Finally, Helpman's earlier monopolistic-competition work sits near the lineage recognised in 2008, and I have not independently verified the priority record.

responses.point: Enflo is less comfortable than I am with treating Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as a caveat. She argues that if the discovery is the empirical facts plus the theory, the credited names are incomplete. She holds that the prize recognises the model that organised the facts and created the welfare channel, and she accepts that this is a judgment about what counts as the discovery.
responses.response: You are right that I treated this too lightly in round 1. Part of my reply is that the model supplies the new object, the selection and reallocation mechanism, and the exporter-premia facts motivated and then tested it. I would not dismiss Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum (2003) as merely complementary, because it is a close contemporaneous model of heterogeneous producers in trade. I therefore rest the defence of the two-name award on a narrower definition of the discovery: selection into exporting and into foreign investment, with its own reallocation channel for gains. The exports-versus-FDI sorting result of Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple has no counterpart in that parallel work, as I read it. I would make that scope explicit in the citation and acknowledge the parallel contributors in the scientific background. If the Committee cannot accept a discovery defined that narrowly, the attribution is genuinely at risk, and I would then move toward B006.

responses.point: Hassler moved from B006 first to B001 first mainly because B001's attribution is cleaner and its discovery boundary tighter. He keeps B006 as his first alternative and says it remains a credible fallback if B001's attribution gap is judged too large. He also notes that B001 and B006 together exceed the three-laureate limit.
responses.response: I agree that B001 and B006 cannot be combined within three people, and a trimmed second part would fragment the BLP credit, so I do not propose a two-part prize. I did not rank B006 in my opening eight, partly because of its boundary. Your move and the discussion since have changed my alternatives. If the Committee can settle the discovery as demand estimation (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes), B006's attribution is tidier than B001's, so I now list B006 as my first alternative. I remain cautious on one point. Its credibility depends on functional-form and instrument assumptions, and I am not in IO, so I cannot judge the out-of-sample evidence. I would want the Committee to weigh that evidence directly, as Dreber Almenberg and Hjalmarsson ask. I still place B001 first because it changed the content of the theory as well as the estimation toolkit, but I treat that as a judgment about kinds of contribution, not an established ordering.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson argues that Eaton-Kortum is a different, Ricardian framework, that Bernard and Jensen's facts motivated rather than replaced the theory, and that the citation should be worded so that it does not overclaim the whole field.
responses.response: I agree on the citation wording and have adopted it. I would qualify the premise. Eaton-Kortum (2002) is Ricardian and distinct, but Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum (2003) is a heterogeneous-producer model with selection into exporting that was developed at about the same time. The parallel contribution is therefore closer than the Eaton-Kortum distinction alone suggests. That does not make the two-name award wrong. It makes the choice of what the discovery is explicit, and the Committee should defend it knowingly, not by treating the omitted names as only motivating facts. The separate exports-versus-FDI sorting result, the monopolistic-competition foundations on the Helpman side and Melitz's tractable aggregation are the parts I would put in the central credit.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee can defend a discovery defined as selection into exporting and foreign investment with a reallocation channel, with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum acknowledged only in the background. If it cannot, a two-name award on this entry may be too narrow.
Whether Redding's quantitative and spatial lineage should be treated as a separate achievement (B037, not on the shortlist) or is part of the credit. I currently treat it as separate.
How much weight Helpman's closeness to the monopolistic-competition work recognised in 2008 should carry in judging incremental novelty.
Whether the welfare implications of the heterogeneous-firm framework are robust enough to appear in the citation. I would keep the wording to selection and reallocation.
Whether B006 can be bounded to the demand-estimation core, and how well structural IO methods hold up out of sample. I have no special expertise there and have not verified it independently.

How to compare the two kinds of contribution, a conceptual reorientation (B001) and a mature methodological toolkit with clean attribution (B006). I weight the first more, but I accept that this is a judgment.

The shared model and reasoning across the eleven files mean the apparent convergence may overstate independent agreement. My assessment rests on the supplied evidence and general knowledge, not independently verified sources.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to Elhanan Helpman or Marc J. Melitz is apparent from my supplied profile. For transparency: I have a long-running collaboration with Peter Klenow (credited in B050, which is neither a preferred part nor an alternative now), frequent co-authorship with Per Krusell and co-authorship with John Hassler, who are also IIES colleagues. I co-authored the Ekonomisk Debatt summaries of the 2024 and 2025 prizes, and the 2025 Scientific Background cites my work. My research on reallocation, creative destruction and misallocation is thematically adjacent to B001 and could bias me toward it, so I disclose that as thematic proximity. None of the credited names in B001, B006 or B030 is a co-author, as far as the profile shows. I disclose these ties and do not adjudicate them.
